characters: Philomena: a 13-year-old girl in a school uniform, with a small purse and a determined look.
Elvis: her best friend, 13, with a notebook, always counting everything.
Madam Ocran: the tuck shop owner, in an apron, behind a counter of snacks and fruit.
The tuck shop: a small wooden stall with biscuits, groundnuts, oranges, bread and cold sachet water, crowded at break time.

narrationPlan.voice: Playful student voices; a calm, kind voice for Madam Ocran
narrationPlan.pace: Quick and funny, like a break-time rush (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Quick, bouncy break-time beat with coin sounds; a calm saving tune near the end (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The students and Madam Ocran are invented. Prices are examples and vary by school and region.
The letter on page 7 is exam-safe: full words, correct spelling, friendly phrases and no chat-style abbreviations.
The story encourages healthy choices without shaming any food or any child’s pocket money.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that the healthy-eating claims (groundnuts for energy and protein; oranges for vitamin C) are accurate and age-appropriate.
Check the idioms (a fool and his money are soon parted; break the bank; lost for words; look out for) with an English teacher for use in informal letters.
Check that prices and the 2-1-1-1 rule are presented as examples.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about budgeting and sharing in a school setting. It teaches a simple spending plan, healthy choices and an exam-safe letter about personal change.
learningGoals: Write an informal letter about a personal habit using full words.
beforeReading: Ask: where does your pocket money go in a week?
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners to find the percentage spent on sweets.
afterReading: Keep a spending diary for one week.
Write a letter to a relative about how you will spend and save.
discussion: Is it better to save, spend or share? Why might we do all three?
Why do we avoid writing “tnx” or “pls” in an exam letter?
reflection: What is one small money habit you could change this week?

mathsExtension.task: Philomena spent GH¢4.50 in ten minutes out of GH¢5. How much was left?
If she saves GH¢1 a day for a five-day school week, how much does she save in four weeks?

support: Give learners a table with columns: Day / Spent / Saved / Shared.
stretch: Plan a class tuck shop that makes a small profit and keeps healthy choices.

culturalNotes: The students and Madam Ocran are invented. Prices are examples and vary by school and region.
The letter on page 7 is exam-safe: full words, correct spelling, friendly phrases and no chat-style abbreviations.
The story encourages healthy choices without shaming any food or any child’s pocket money.
localiseThis: Use real local prices and foods; follow your school’s rules about tuck shops and food safety.

factCheck.claim: Informal letters use full, friendly language with a clear introduction, body and conclusion; common closings include “Yours ever” and “Your loving friend”.
factCheck.explanation: From a Ghana curriculum learning-material lesson on informal letters.
factCheck.reference: Ghana curriculum resources, “English Language LM Year 1 Section 15”.

factCheck.claim: Texting abbreviations such as “b4”, “dat” and “@” for “at” have been reported to lose marks in WASSCE formal letters.
factCheck.explanation: From a Junior Graphic article reporting on examiners (2015). The same issue was raised by WAEC again in September 2026.
factCheck.reference: Junior Graphic, “Youngsters’ abbreviated words and exam results”; MyJoyOnline, “Social media language creeping into students’ examination scripts: WAEC” (7 September 2026).
